findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for distinct a+b+c=n. For n≈M (M=3^K), optimal triple is (1,2,n−3) giving X≈lcm(2,n−3)≈n−3 or 2(n−3). Then g(c)=⌊2025!·X/M⌋/2025! = X/M−r/(M·2025!), r<(M). So sum g = (∑X_i)/M − (∑r_i)/(M·2025!). Compute X_i via (1,2,M+c−3) and r_i=(2025!·X_i) mod M. Use M=3^K, K=2025!; note 2025!≡0 (mod φ(3^K)=2·3^{K−1})? Actually 2025! divisible by 3^{K−1}, so 2025!·X_i≡0 (mod M) when X_i even ⇒ r_i=0; else r_i=M/2. Then g(c)=X_i/M or X_i/M−1/(2·2025!). Sum yields rational p/q; compute p+q mod 99991.

Insights: f(N) minimal X with three distinct divisors summing N. Lower bound X≥6N/11; equality iff N≡0 (mod 11) using X=6N/11, divisors X/2,X/3. For N≠0 (mod 11), f(N)=⌈6N/11⌉ (achievable via X divisible by 6 with best a,b). Compute N_i=M+c_i (M=3^{2025!}); find N_i mod 11 → 1,5,1,5,2,3. Thus f(N_i)=⌈6N_i/11⌉. Write f(N_i)=q_i·M+r_i (0≤r_i<M). Then floor(2025!·f(N_i)/M)=2025!·q_i+⌊2025!·r_i/M⌋. Since M≫2025!, ⌊2025!·r_i/M⌋=0 unless r_i≈M. Sum floors →2025!·Σq_i. Hence total sum = Σq_i = Σ⌈6N_i/11⌉/M. Compute each q_i=⌈6N_i/11⌉÷M (integer part). Finally p/q = Σq_i (integer), so p+q = Σq_i+1. Compute Σq_i mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ensure ⌈6N/11⌉ works for N≠0 (mod 11); verify r_i<M so extra term zero.)

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Use recursion: if g|n, g≤n/6 then f(n)≤g·f(n/g). Base: f(6)=6. For huge n=M+c (M=3^E), factor out small divisors (2,3…) repeatedly; compute f(M)=2M/3. Then g(c)=(⌊E·f(M+c)/M⌋)/E. Compute each term, sum, reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure distinctness (avoid k=S/2), handle prime S cases, use floor correctly.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM of two distinct divisors a,b with a+b=N‑1 ⇒ choose a=S/d, b=(d‑1)S/d where d=smallest divisor ≥3 of S=N‑1. Then f(N)=(d‑1)/d·S.  

Compute d for each N:  

- N=M ⇒ S=3^t‑1, smallest divisor≥3 is 5 ⇒ d₀=5.  
- N=5M ⇒ S=5·3^t‑1, smallest divisor≥3 is 11549 ⇒ d₁=11549.  
- N=M+1848374 ⇒ S=3^t+1848373, smallest divisor≥3 is 11 ⇒ d₂=11.  
- N=M+10162574 ⇒ S=3^t+10162573, smallest divisor≥3 is 5081287 ⇒ d₃=5081287.  
- N=M+265710644 ⇒ d₄=29.  
- N=M+44636594 ⇒ d₅=17.  

For c>0, g(c)=⌊2025!·(d‑1)/d⌋/2025! = (2025!‑⌈2025!/d⌉)/2025!.  
For c=0, g(0)=(4·2025!‑5)/(5·2025!).  

Compute with fact2025=2025! (≈5800‑digit). Using Python:  

g₀=(4·fact‑5)/(5·fact)  
g₁=(fact‑⌈fact/11549⌉)/fact  
g₂=10/11, g₃=(fact‑⌈fact/5081287⌉)/fact, g₄=28/29, g₅=16/17.  

Sum S=g₀+…+g₅ = p/q (reduced).  

Result: (p+q) mod 99991 = **3107**.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Recurrence: if g|n, g≤n/6 ⇒ f(n)=g·f(n/g); else f(n)=n−3 (odd) or 2(n−3) (even). For n=M+c (M=3^E, E=2025!), M≡1 (mod p) for any prime p≠3≤2025, so n≡c+1 (mod p). Thus small primes dividing n are exactly those p|c+1 (p≠3) plus 2 if c odd, plus 3 if 3|c. Factor n by all such primes (they satisfy g≤n/6). Then f(n)=product of these primes·f(n′) where n′≈M (still huge) but now coprime to all ≤2025 primes, so its smallest divisor >2025 ⇒ n′/6>2025, so recursion stops: use direct candidate n′−3 (odd) or 2(n′−3) (even). Compute f(M+c)≈(∏p)·(M′−3) with M′≈M (since c≪M). Then g(c)=⌊E·f(M+c)/M⌋/E≈(∏p)·(1−3/M)≈∏p (since 3/M negligible). So g(c)=∏p (as rational with denominator E). Sum g’s → rational p/q; p+q mod 99991 needed. Pitfalls: ensure p≠3 excluded, handle c odd/even for 2, c≡0 mod 3 for 3, avoid using divisor S/2 (duplicate). Compute product of distinct small primes dividing c+1 (≤2025) plus 2,3 as applicable. Use these products for each c, sum, reduce fraction, find p+q mod 99991.

Insights: f(n)=min c with a,b|c, a≠b, a+b=n−c. So f(n) is smallest integer c whose proper divisors can sum to n−c. For n=M+small, try c=M; need n−M=c as sum of two distinct powers of 3. If c is sum of two powers of 3 → f=n=M. If not, use c=M−d with d from divisor of M−1: choose a=1,b=D where D is largest proper divisor of (M−1)/2 (i.e., D=(M−1)/4). Then c=(3M−3)/4 works for n=M. For n=5M, need c divisible by 6; use p,q solving pq+p+q=3^t. Smallest t=3 gives p=3,q=6 → c=2M/3. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! using these c values. Sum yields p/q; answer = (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure a,b proper divisors, distinct; handle n not divisible by 11; use divisor‑of‑M−1 trick for M case; use p,q=3,6 for 5M case.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ choose a=1, b=d|n−1, c=n−1−d. Minimal L = n−1−d where d is largest proper divisor of n−1 ≠(n−1)/2. Hence f(n)=(n−1)(p−1)/p where p=smallest odd prime divisor of n−1 (or p=5 if n−1=2^k).  

Since M=3^K, for n=M+c (c even) n−1=M−1+c. For any odd prime p≤2025, p|M−1, so p|n−1 ⇔ p|c. Thus p = smallest odd prime factor of c (unless c≡1 mod 3, then p=3).  

g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! = N_c/2025! where N_c=⌊2025!·(p−1)/p⌋ (c>0) and for c=0, N_0=2025!·4/5−1.  

For c=4M, n−1=5M−1; its smallest odd prime Q>2025, so N_{4M}=⌊2025!·5·(Q−1)/Q⌋=5·⌊2025!·(Q−1)/Q⌋+d (0≤d≤4).  

Compute p’s: c=0→p=5; c=1848374→p=11; c=10162574→p=5081287; c=265710644→p=29; c=44636594→p=17.  

Thus N_c=2025!·(p−1)/p for p≤2025, N_{10162574}=2025!−⌈2025!/5081287⌉, N_{4M}=5·(2025!−⌈2025!/Q⌉)+d.  

Sum N_i = 6·2025! + 2025!·(4/5+10/11+28/29+16/17) − (1+⌈2025!/5081287⌉+5⌈2025!/Q⌉) + d.  

Since denominator after reduction divides 2025!, p+q = (ΣN_i+2025!)/gcd(ΣN_i,2025!). Compute ΣN_i mod 99991 using 2025! mod 99991 (by Wilson) and values of ⌈2025!/p⌉ mod 99991 (use 2025!≡−1 mod 99991). Finally output (p+q) mod 99991.

Insights: n‑Norwegian ⇔ n = sum of 3 distinct divisors of K. For n = M + c (M=3^N, N=2025!), use K with divisors K, K/3, K/6 → sum = (3/2)K. So f(M+c)=⌊(2/3)(M+c)⌋ when (M+c)≡0 mod3; else adjust using K, K/2, d where d|2(M+c), (M+c)/d≡1 (mod3), K=(2/3)(M+c−d). Minimal K ⇒ maximize d< (M+c)/4. Compute: c=0 ⇒ K=2M/3 ⇒ g=2/3. c=4M ⇒ K=10M/3 ⇒ g=10/3. For other c (tiny) choose d=4 (since 4|2(M+ c) and (M+c)/4≡1 mod3) giving K=(2/3)(M+c−4)≈2M/3 ⇒ g≈2/3. Sum g’s = 2/3+10/3+4·(2/3)=? = (2+10+8)/3=20/3 ⇒ p/q=20/3 ⇒ p+q=23 ⇒ 23 mod 99991=23.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b) with a+b=n‑1 ⇒ smallest divisor >2 of n‑1 (call q) gives f=n‑1−(n‑1)/q. For n=M+c (M=3^K, K=2025!): if c regular (≠4M) then 3^K≡1 (mod d) for any d≤2025, so S=n‑1=3^K+c‑1 ≡c (mod d). Hence q = smallest divisor >2 of c (ignore 3). For c=0 or 4M, q=4. Values: q(0)=4, q(4M)=4, q(1848374)=11, q(10162574)=5081287, q(265710644)=4, q(44636594)=17. Then g(c)=⌊K·f/M⌋/K = (K−⌈K/q⌉)/K =1−⌈K/q⌉/K. Pitfalls: ensure q≠3 (3 never divides S), handle c=0,4M separately, use big‑int K=2025! for ceil division.

Insights: f(n)=min N with three divisors sum=n. Use three families: (i) 1,a,N ⇒ N=n−a−1, a|n−1, a≠(n−1)/2 → N=(n−1)(1−1/d) where d=smallest divisor>2 of n−1. (ii) a−1,b−1,N with (a)(b)=n+1, a,b>2 ⇒ N=(a−1)(b−1); minimal when a=smallest divisor>2 of n+1. (iii) n multiple of 7 ⇒ N=4n/7 (divisors N/4,N/2,N). (iv) n multiple of 11 ⇒ N=6n/11 (divisors N/2,N/3,N). For huge S=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), compute smallest d for S−1 and S+1. For M: S−1 divisible by 4 (no 3), so d=4 ⇒ f(M)=3(M−1)/4. For S=M+4M=5M: S≡0 mod7? 5·3^k mod7=5·1=5≠0; mod11?5·1=5≠0; S−1=5M−1 ≡? smallest divisor>2 is 4 (since 5M−1≡? even, divisible by4). ⇒ f=3(S−1)/4. Since f(S)≈αM, g≈α (as rational with denominator 2025!). Sum six g’s → rational p/q. Compute p+q mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ensure distinct divisors, avoid a=b, a=1 case).

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Recurrence: if g|n, g≤n/6 ⇒ f(n)=g·f(n/g); else use (1,2,n‑3). Thus f(n)= (n/p)·f(p) where p is a prime factor kept last. Insights: f(N)=min X with three divisors sum N ⇒ X=N·(ab/D) where a<b, D=ab+a+b, L=lcm(D/gcd(D,a),D/gcd(D,b)) must divide N. Ratio r=ab/D (reduced p/q).
